newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HORSE RACING-FIVE CHARGED IN HK BETTING SCANDAL.
newsitem.headline: HORSE RACING-FIVE CHARGED IN HK BETTING SCANDAL.

text.p: Hong Kong graft busters charged five people on Tuesday with taking illegal bets and the Jockey Club vowed a clean-up campaign as one of this British colony's worst horse racing scandals gathered steam.

The five appeared in the district court after being charged by the Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC) with illegal bookmaking linked to a fiasco in which 37 people have been hauled in for questioning in the past two days.
Two of the five were Malaysian citizens and three were Hong Kong residents. All pleaded not guilty and were released on bail. They will appear in court again on May 16.
The charges stem from the biggest race fixing and illegal betting scandal on Hong Kong's race courses. None of the other 32 people questioned have been charged so far.
The ICAC said earlier it had freed on bail 19 of the people it originally detained, but the probe was far from over.
The Malaysians charged were named as Yong Seng-Chen and Liew Siew-cheong. The three Hong Kong residents were Chan Hung-yip, Kam Tat-Fai and Ching Fuk-hung. Occupations were not stated.
The Malaysians were released on bail of HK$750,000 (US$96,200) each in cash, and the Hong Kong defendants were released on bail of HK$100,000 each.

The Jockey Club, which has a monopoly on horse racing and gaming in the territory, said it would go ahead with this weekend's races despite the turmoil caused by the biggest race fixing inquiry in more than a decade.
"The Hong Kong Jockey Club is determined to keep horse racing clean," Wilson Cheng, the club's information secretary, told Reuters.
"Racing will continue as scheduled on Saturday," he said.
Cheng also said the club would not suspend any jockeys and trainers due to take part in this Saturday's race meeting unless they were actually incriminated by the (ICAC) investigation.
"After we hear more from the ICAC, our stewards will take appropriate actions," he said.
On Monday the ICAC said 37 people had been arrested, including five jockeys, two trainers and three Jockey Club staff. On Tuesday 18 were still being questioned, it said.
The ICAC cannot hold detainees longer than 48 hours without bringing charges.

The races are the only legal outlet for a flutter on the horses in gambling-mad Hong Kong. Horse racing is one of the biggest businesses in the territory of 6.4 million people, outperforming some weighty blue chip companies in turnover.
Betting turnover in the 1995/96 season was HK$80 billion (US$11 billion), believed the highest per capita in the world.

The ICAC probe was front-page news and diverted the public eye away from the political polemics and Sino-British wrangling as China gets ready to take the territory back from Britain at midnight on June 30.
Editorialists and cartoonists had a field day. Many of them sang the praises of the ICAC and the Jockey Club for acting swiftly to protect fair racing.
"In the long run, the Jockey Club's determination to act will boost local and international confidence," the independent daily Ming Pao said.
A cartoon in the English-language South China Morning Post showed an ICAC troubleshooter wearing a gas mask entering the stables to eliminate a foul odour.
